speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: Welcome to our Brexit Watch podcast. I'll look behind the headlines after Britain's decision to leave the EU and in the immediate aftermath of that referendum, much consternation across the Atlantic in terms of how the United States economy might be affected by Britain's departure from the European Union. Britain is the biggest foreign investor in the United States, making up 15% of foreign direct investment ahead of Canada, China and Japan. And the US is the biggest export market for the UK, receiving more than $31 billion worth of British goods each year. So when President Barack Obama issued a stark warning that a UK outside the EU would go to the back of the queue in trade relations with America, alarm bells sounded, there was a feeling, especially among pro-leave politicians, that President Obama was disrespecting the special relationship in favour of cultivating ties with the leaders of Germany and France. Well, how much has changed since the election of Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress? There is now considerable momentum for a US-UK bilateral trade deal. After the Brexit vote, Mr Trump had promised to strengthen our ties with a free and independent Britain, deepening our bonds in commerce, culture and mutual defence to quote him. And there are already no less than five pieces of congressional legislation calling for an Anglo-American free trade deal. most prominent being the United Kingdom Trade Continuity Act, introduced in the Senate by Mike Lee of Utah and Tom Cotton of Arkansas, both rising stars in the Republican Party. I spoke to Senator Lee about his views on how Brexit will impact Britain's relationship with the United States economy.
